cells.label: fact

items.text: Bank of America states that emerging technologies and the growth of e-commerce have allowed non-traditional financial service providers and technology companies to compete by offering electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions, and that increased competition may reduce its fee-based revenue through pricing pressure.
items.quote: allowed non-traditional financial service providers and technology companies to compete with traditional financial service companies in providing electronic and internet-based financial solutions and services, including electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it has experienced and may continue to experience pricing pressures as some competitors seek market share by reducing prices and fees, eliminating commissions, or providing more favorable terms of business.
items.quote: some of our competitors seek to obtain market share by reducing prices and fees, paying higher interest rates on deposits, eliminating commissions or other fees or otherwise providing more favorable terms of business

items.text: Charles Schwab states that its industry is highly competitive and characterized by aggressive price competition.
items.quote: Our industry is highly competitive and characterized by aggressive price competition.

items.text: A trade press source attributes platform fees at major distributors to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry, as distributors need to replace transaction revenue.
items.quote: all these platform tolls showing up at the giant distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry. The revenue replacement has to come from somewhere

items.text: A trade press source notes that major wires introduced data fees to offset declining transaction revenue, with an analyst first predicting widespread adoption of data fees when Schwab began charging for data it had provided free.
items.quote: major wires, including UBS and Wells Fargo introduced data fees in the mid-2010s, and 2020, respectively... Pirker first predicted the widespread adoption of data fees to offset declining transaction revenue in 2019

items.text: A Morgan Stanley executive notes press coverage highlighting efforts by smaller RIAs employing more aggressive pricing to compete for workplace business, a sign of evolving competitive pressure on pricing.
items.quote: There was some press coverage this quarter, just highlighting efforts by smaller RIAs, employing more aggressive pricing to compete for some of that business

items.text: Raymond James states it competes on pricing, including execution pricing and fee levels, among other factors.
items.quote: We compete on the basis of a number of factors, including the quality of our associates and financial advisors, our products and services, pricing (such as execution pricing and fee levels)

items.text: A trade press source states that the SEC's sustained focus on cash sweep disclosures, combined with litigation against firms over low client yields, keeps the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash a live issue driving transparency.
items.quote: The SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures, combined with a wave of litigation against major firms over allegedly low client yields, means that the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash is unlikely to fade from client conversations

items.text: A survey found that nearly half (48%) of participants consider pricing and overall anticipated cost among the top factors in choosing an advisor, and that pricing clarity can be a dealbreaker, reflecting client-driven pressure for fee transparency.
items.quote: Nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others... Pricing clarity can be a dealbreaker (or deal maker).

cells.reason: Multiple sources explicitly describe competitive pricing pressure (low/no-fee competitors, commission elimination, aggressive pricing, data/shelf fees replacing transaction revenue) and transparency pressure (SEC sweep scrutiny, litigation, client demand for pricing clarity) driving fee changes and transparency.
